sheets.name: Course Description
rows: This course introduces students to the foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on how modern transformer-based systems can understand, retrieve, and generate information. It emphasizes conceptual clarity around tokenization, embeddings, attention, and the distinction between proprietary and open-source models, while also developing practical skills in prompt engineering and API integration. Beginning with core concepts of LLMs and prompt design, students gradually progress to building Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, working with vector databases, and designing agentic AI workflows that use tools, memory, and planning. The course further develops competence in deploying LLM-powered applications using web frameworks and containerization, alongside responsible AI practices around safety, privacy, and governance. By the end, learners will be capable of designing, implementing, and evaluating end-to-end AI systems that combine LLMs, retrieval, and agents for real-world applications.

The primary objectives of this course are to develop a comprehensive understanding of Generative AI, transformer-based Large Language Models, and their practical application in building intelligent systems. It aims to enable students to design effective prompts, integrate LLM APIs with appropriate sampling parameters, and construct robust RAG pipelines using embeddings, chunking strategies, and vector databases for reliable information retrieval. The course encourages analytical thinking through the evaluation of agentic AI architectures, including tool/function calling, memory mechanisms, planning strategies, and multi-agent coordination patterns. Students will also learn to design and deploy secure, observable, and scalable AI applications using frameworks such as FastAPI, Streamlit/Gradio, and Docker, while incorporating guardrails and ethical safeguards. Ultimately, the course equips learners with the applied AI engineering competence required to build, assess, and responsibly adopt LLM-, RAG-, and agent-based solutions in academic and industry contexts.
Understand the fundamental concepts of Generative AI, Transformer architecture (tokenization, embeddings, attention), and the distinction between proprietary and open-source Large Language Models
Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought) and integrate LLM APIs with appropriate sampling parameters to build functional conversational applications

Analyze data retrieval requirements and construct end-to-end Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines involving embeddings, chunking, vector databases, retrieval, and reranking, while evaluating output faithfulness

Evaluate agentic AI architectures involving tool/function calling, memory systems, planning strategies, multi-agent coordination, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based integrations, judging their suitability for a given task
Design and deploy secure, production-ready AI applications using FastAPI, Streamlit/Gradio, Docker, and CI/CD workflows, incorporating guardrails and observability mechanisms
Critically evaluate AI ethics, security, privacy, and governance principles, and appraise emerging trends (on-device LLMs, RAG-agent integration, MCP ecosystems) for responsible AI adoption

sheets.name: Session Plan
rows: Understand the fundamental concepts of Generative AI, Transformer architecture, and Large Language Models
Unit I: Foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models
Generative AI: Concepts, Scope, and Foundation Models

Introduce Generative AI by having students list familiar AI use cases (chatbots, image generators) and classify which are generative vs traditional ML, then walk through how foundation models are trained and used in practice.

Concept Mapping: Create a one-page concept map that contrasts traditional ML with Generative AI and Large Language Models. Use a concrete example (e.g., FAQ chatbot vs LLM assistant) to highlight differences in data requirements, capabilities, and limitations.
Transformer Architecture: Tokenization, Embeddings, and Attention Mechanism
Walk through the transformer pipeline step-by-step using simple sentences, visualizing tokenization, embeddings, and attention with diagrams and an interactive demo from an LLM playground.

Short Reflective Essay: Write a 500-word reflection explaining tokenization and embeddings, using an analogy from daily life (e.g., words as ingredients, embeddings as flavor profiles). Include how these concepts impact retrieval and generation quality.
Attention Is All You Need (Explained) (Jay Alammar / The Illustrated Transformer)
Proprietary and Open-Source Language Models: A Comparative Study

Facilitate a guided comparison where students investigate documentation pages of proprietary (e.g., OpenAI, Gemini) and open-source (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral) models in small groups and summarize trade-offs on cost, control, and deployment.
Model Access Paradigms: Cloud-Hosted APIs and Local Deployment (Ollama, Hugging Face)
Demonstrate both cloud-hosted and local model access by showing API calls in a notebook and a local run via Ollama, then have students map when each paradigm is suitable for different constraints.
Apply prompt engineering principles and LLM API integration to develop functional AI applications
Unit II: Prompt Engineering and LLM API Integration
Anatomy of a Prompt: System, User, and Assistant Roles; Context Window
Use live demos in an LLM playground to rewrite the same task with different system and user instructions, highlighting how role separation and context window size affect behavior and memory.

Prompt Design Portfolio: Create at least 6 prompts (2 per role) showcasing zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought patterns. For each, show the system prompt, user prompt, and at least one sample response with brief commentary on why the prompt works.
Prompting Techniques: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought, and Structured Output Generation
Run interactive exercises where students iteratively refine prompts from zero-shot to few-shot to chain-of-thought, and finally request structured JSON, comparing outputs for the same task.

API Integration Task: Implement a Python script that takes text input, calls an LLM API (OpenAI/Gemini or local via Ollama), and prints a concise bullet-point summary. Include configuration via environment variables for API keys and parameters.
Introduction to Tool-Oriented and Function-Calling Prompts
Show examples of tool/function calling payloads and role-play “LLM as coordinator” in class, having students decide when to call which tool given a natural language request.

Prompt Robustness Study: Choose a fixed task (e.g., explanation of binary search) and systematically vary temperature/top-p. Collect outputs in a table and write a 700-word analysis of how style, coherence, and variability change.
LLM API Fundamentals: Authentication, Rate Limits, and Sampling Parameters (Temperature, Top-p, Max Tokens)
Walk through a simple Python notebook calling an LLM API, then have students experiment with temperature and top-p settings and observe changes in determinism and creativity.
Practical Exercise: Development of a Conversational Chatbot using LLM API and Web Interface
Guide students step-by-step to build a minimal conversational chatbot in Python using Streamlit or Gradio, wiring it to an LLM API and iteratively improving prompts.
Analyze information retrieval requirements and design end-to-end Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines
Unit III: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Embeddings, and Evaluation
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Architecture and Workflow (Ingestion, Indexing, Retrieval, Generation)
Use a block-diagram walkthrough to explain each RAG stage, then have students collaboratively sketch an architecture for a “Department Handbook Assistant” on the whiteboard.

RAG Design Document: Draw and explain an architecture showing data ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector store, retrieval, reranking, and answer generation. Specify tools (e.g., LangChain/LlamaIndex, ChromaDB/FAISS) and justify design choices.
Embeddings: Vector Representation of Text and Similarity Measures
Demonstrate embeddings by projecting example sentences into 2D (using a notebook) and visually clustering similar meanings, then relate cosine similarity to “angle between meanings”.

Implementation Assignment: Build a Python app that ingests at least one multi-page PDF, chunks it, stores embeddings in a vector DB, and answers user questions via a simple CLI or web UI. Include basic logging of queries and answers.
Document Chunking Strategies: Fixed-Length, Semantic, and Hierarchical Approaches
Present a long sample document and have students experiment with different chunking strategies, discussing trade-offs for context, overlap, and retrieval quality.

RAG Evaluation Task: Prepare at least 15 domain-specific questions, run them on both “LLM-only” and your RAG system, and manually rate answers for correctness and faithfulness. Summarize results in charts and a short report.
Vector Database Systems: ChromaDB, FAISS, and Pinecone
Compare vector databases conceptually by showing their APIs and deployment models, then run a simple similarity search demo using one local and one managed option.
Information Retrieval Techniques: Hybrid Search, Top-k Retrieval, and Maximal Marginal Relevance
Use visual examples to show dense vs keyword vs hybrid search results for the same query and discuss when diversity (MMR) is helpful for reducing redundancy.
Reranking Methods: Cross-Encoder and LLM-Based Reranking
Explain reranking by walking through an example where initial retrieved passages are reordered by a stronger model, then analyze before/after answer quality.
Evaluation of RAG Systems: Faithfulness, Hallucination Rate, and Latency Metrics
Run a live demo where the RAG system occasionally hallucinates, then have students label outputs for faithfulness and discuss metrics and trade-offs with latency.
Evaluate and design agentic AI systems incorporating tool use, memory, planning, and multi-agent coordination
Unit IV: Agentic AI, Tool Integration, and Multi-Agent Systems
AI Agents: Definition, Autonomy, and Agentic Control Loops
Introduce AI agents by contrasting simple chat completion with loop-based agent execution, drawing a control loop diagram and walking through an example task.

Tool Schema Design: Specify JSON schemas (parameters, types, descriptions, constraints) for each tool so that an LLM can call them reliably. Include 3 example prompts and expected tool call JSON for each.
Tool Calling and Function Calling: Schema Design and Error Handling
Show real logs of successful and failed tool calls and have students identify schema/design issues and propose better parameter descriptions and validation.

Single-Agent Tool-Using Demo: Using LangChain/LangGraph or similar, implement an agent with at least two tools: a search-like tool (real or stubbed) and a RAG tool over a small document set. Demonstrate multi-step reasoning for 5 queries.
Memory Architectures in AI Agents: Short-Term, Long-Term, Episodic, and Semantic Memory
Use a whiteboard analogy to map human memory types to concrete agent memory stores (conversation buffer, vector store, logs), then examine how memory impacts behavior.

Multi-Agent Workflow Design: Define roles (e.g., Researcher, Summarizer, Critic), responsibilities, communication protocol, and failure-handling strategy. Represent the workflow as a sequence diagram with narrative explanation.
Planning in AI Agents: Task Decomposition, Planner-Executor Pattern, and Self-Reflection
Demonstrate a planner-executor agent run and annotate each step, then have students manually decompose a complex task into subtasks and critique the plan.
Multi-Agent Systems: Agent Roles and Coordination Strategies
Organize a classroom role-play where students act as different agents (Researcher, Summarizer, Critic) passing messages to solve a task, then map this to a multi-agent graph.
Model Context Protocol (MCP): Standardized Framework for Tool and Data Access
Explain MCP concepts via an architecture diagram showing models, tools, and data services connected through a common protocol, then discuss interoperability benefits.
Anthropic MCP Documentation; Google Cloud MCP Guide
Design and deploy secure, ethically compliant AI applications following responsible AI principles
Unit V: AI Application Deployment, Governance, and Responsible AI
AI Application Design Patterns: Conversational Agents, Support Systems, and Research Assistants
Present several real-world LLM app case studies and have students identify the underlying design pattern and key components (front-end, LLM, tools, storage).

Deployment Plan: Describe target environment (server/on-prem/cloud), API gateway, authentication, logging, metrics, alerting, and versioning strategy for prompts and models. Include a simple CI/CD outline using GitHub.
AI Guardrails: Content Filtering, Safety Checks, and Adversarial Prompt Mitigation
Demonstrate prompt injection and unsafe outputs in a controlled setting, then layer content filters, policies, and system prompts to mitigate them and discuss remaining risks.

Containerization & API Assignment: Expose a /generate endpoint that calls an LLM (hosted or local), package the app in a Docker image, and provide steps to run it locally. Include basic request validation and error responses.
AI System Observability: Logging, Latency Monitoring, and Prompt Version Control
Show observability dashboards and log samples from an LLM app, then have students identify what should be monitored for reliability, cost, and safety.

Ethics & Safety Case Study: Given a short case describing potential misuse in an educational or enterprise setting, write a 1500-word analysis covering risks, stakeholders, mitigation strategies (prompting, filters, access control), and monitoring.
Deployment Architecture: FastAPI, Streamlit/Gradio, Docker, and Continuous Integration
Live-code a small FastAPI or Streamlit endpoint backed by an LLM, then containerize it with Docker and explain how CI/CD would automate builds and deployment.

Policy Brief on Emerging Trends: Summarize key trends (on-device LLMs, RAG+agents, MCP ecosystem), opportunities, risks, and recommended guidelines for student/faculty use in 2–3 pages targeted at HOD/principal.
AI Ethics, Security, and Privacy: Data Governance, Personal Data Protection, and Algorithmic Bias
Use real or hypothetical case studies to debate ethical failures, then map each scenario to concrete governance measures like data policies, audits, and consent mechanisms.
Emerging Trends in AI: On-Device Language Models, RAG-Agent Integration, and MCP Ecosystems

Facilitate a trends discussion where students research and present short spotlights on on-device LLMs, advanced RAG+agents, and MCP ecosystems, then synthesize implications for education and industry.

sheets.name: Course Description
rows: Foundations of AI, ML & Data Science

This course is designed to introduce learners to the foundational concepts of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science, focusing on their evolution, core principles, and real-world applications. The course covers essential topics such as AI vs ML vs DL, data types and data sources, data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, basic machine learning concepts, and model evaluation metrics. It also emphasizes ethical, legal, and governance considerations in AI, along with practical exposure to Python-based data science tools. The course aims to build conceptual clarity, analytical thinking, and application-oriented understanding for data-driven problem solving.

This course equips learners with fundamental knowledge and practical understanding of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science, enabling them to work with data, apply basic analytical and machine learning techniques, interpret results effectively, follow responsible AI practices, and develop readiness for advanced learning and career pathways in AI and data-driven domains.

History and evolution of AI – origins in 1950s, Turing Test, symbolic AI, expert systems, AI winters, resurgence with big data and GPUs, modern generative AI
Build a physical wall timeline of AI milestones as a class, then discuss why each AI winter happened and what ended it.

Interview a person over 50 (parent, grandparent or senior faculty) about what 'thinking machines' meant in their youth. Hand-draw an AI timeline on chart paper and annotate it with their recollections.
Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig
AI vs ML vs DL – definition and scope, rule-based vs data-driven systems, supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, deep architectures, real-world examples
Use nested physical containers (box inside box inside box) to make the AI/ML/DL containment relationship concrete, then classify live examples together.

Collect 10 printed clippings (newspaper, magazine, product packaging, poster) that use the word 'AI'. Classify each as rule-based, ML, DL or marketing hype and paste them on chart paper with a written justification.
AI in healthcare, finance, retail – medical diagnosis and imaging, fraud detection and credit scoring, recommendation systems, demand forecasting, customer analytics
Have students map AI use cases to businesses they physically visit, so the applications stop being abstract vendor examples.

Visit a local clinic, bank branch or kirana store. Ask staff which three decisions still depend on human judgement. Present a 2-minute oral pitch on which of them AI could assist and which it should not.
Agent types and environments – simple reflex agents, model-based agents, goal-based agents, learning agents, observable vs partially observable environments, deterministic vs stochastic
Classify household devices as agents in class, arguing over borderline cases such as a washing machine versus a robot vacuum.

Pick four devices in your home (thermostat, washing machine, TV recommender, geyser, robot vacuum). Hand-draw a table classifying each by agent type and by environment properties, then defend one borderline case in writing.
State space, search concepts – state representation, initial and goal states, search trees and graphs, BFS and DFS, heuristic search, optimality and completeness
Lay a maze on the classroom floor with tape and chairs, then have students physically walk BFS and DFS to feel the difference in node expansion.
Build a maze on the floor using tape, books or chairs. Walk it once as BFS and once as DFS, filming both runs. Count the steps taken and hand-draw the resulting search tree.

Walk the six CRISP-DM phases against a live campus problem so students see the loop back from evaluation to business understanding.

Choose a real problem faced by a campus club (predicting event attendance, canteen wastage, library crowding). Write the six CRISP-DM phases on paper for that problem and get one club office-bearer to sign off on the business understanding phase.
Structured vs unstructured data – tabular datasets, relational databases, text data, images and videos, challenges in preprocessing, feature extraction
Empty a bag onto the desk and sort the contents into structured, semi-structured and unstructured piles, arguing over receipts and handwritten notes.

Collect 20 real artefacts from your bag and phone (receipts, tickets, photos, chat screenshots, notes, voice memos). Sort them on a physical grid into structured, semi-structured and unstructured, then note one preprocessing challenge per category.
APIs, databases, sensors – REST APIs, data collection pipelines, SQL and NoSQL databases, IoT sensors, real-time data ingestion
Have students act as a human sensor and a human ingestion pipeline for 24 hours, then compare the failure modes with automated pipelines.

Log one real sensor reading every hour for 24 hours by hand (room temperature, phone battery, step count, noise level). Document the collection process, every missed reading and the reason it was missed.
Apply data science workflow concepts including CRISP-DM, structured vs unstructured data, data sources, data cleaning, and handling missing values using real-world datasets
Data cleaning concepts – duplicate removal, noise handling, consistency checks, data validation, data quality improvement
Distribute a printed, deliberately corrupted attendance or marks sheet and have students colour-code every defect before touching a keyboard.
Given a printed messy attendance sheet, mark every data quality defect with a colour code (duplicate, inconsistent format, impossible value, missing) and hand-write a cleaning rulebook for the sheet.
Python for Data Analysis by Wes McKinney
Handling missing values – deletion methods, mean and median imputation, forward and backward filling, predictive imputation
Have students impute gaps in their own personal log, so they can judge which method distorts a reality they actually remember.

Keep a handwritten daily log of your own sleep or expenses for one week, leaving the genuine gaps in place. Apply deletion, mean imputation, median imputation and forward fill by hand and in a notebook, then argue which distorts your real week least.
EDA objectives and methods – understanding data distribution, detecting patterns, identifying anomalies, hypothesis generation, visualization techniques
Ask students to write their questions before opening the data, then confront how many the data can actually answer.

Export your own phone screen-time report. Before looking at it, write five questions you expect it to answer. Then examine it and report, orally, which questions it could and could not answer and why.
Mean, median, variance – measures of central tendency, dispersion analysis, skewed data interpretation, robustness of median
Collect a real measurement from the whole class, compute the statistics on the board by hand, then insert one extreme value and watch the mean move while the median holds.

Measure one real physical quantity 30 times (heights of classmates, time to walk to the canteen, weight of your bag each day). Compute mean, median and variance by hand, then add one extreme value and recompute.
An Introduction to Statistical Learning by James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani
Bar, line, histogram plots – categorical comparison, time-series visualization, frequency distribution, trend analysis
Have students hand-draw the three chart types on graph paper first, then reproduce them in Python and compare what each encoding reveals and hides.

Using your own 30 days of screen-time or expense data, hand-draw a bar chart, a line chart and a histogram on graph paper. Reproduce all three in Python and write which chart revealed something the others hid.
Analyse exploratory data analysis techniques including descriptive statistics, data visualization, outlier detection, trends, and insight generation for decision-making
Outliers, trends – anomaly detection, box plots, trend identification, impact on model performance
Send students to collect real daily counts from a local vendor, then have them take the detected outliers back to the vendor for explanation.

Collect daily footfall, sales or price data from a local vendor for seven days. Identify outliers using a hand-drawn box plot, then return to the vendor and ask what caused each outlier. Record the explanation.
Insight generation – pattern interpretation, business relevance, decision support, actionable recommendations
Swap datasets between students so each must generate recommendations for a business they did not visit, then compare with the collector's own reading.

Exchange your seven-day vendor dataset with a peer. Write three actionable recommendations for their vendor. Compare your recommendations with the ones written by the student who actually visited the shop.
Explain the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science including history, evolution, AI vs ML vs DL, agent types, and real-world applications

Build a cause-effect diagram for a campus outcome everyone experiences, and argue over which arrows are genuinely causal.

Choose a real campus outcome (late assignment submissions, low attendance in the first lecture, canteen queue length). Hand-draw a cause-effect diagram, mark dependent and independent variables, and mark which arrows you cannot justify.
An Introduction to Statistical Learning by James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani
Random variables & distributions – discrete and continuous variables, normal distribution, binomial distribution, probability density
Run a physical randomness experiment in class, tally by hand and compare the empirical distribution against the theoretical one.

Perform 200 trials of a physical random experiment (dice rolls, coin flips, drawing chits). Tally results by hand, plot the empirical distribution on graph paper and compare it with the theoretical distribution.
Apply data science workflow concepts including CRISP-DM, structured vs unstructured data, data sources, data cleaning, and handling missing values using real-world datasets
Simple probability problems – basic probability rules, conditional probability, real-life decision examples
Set a closed-book in-class problem set built from data the class itself collected in earlier sessions.
Closed-book, in-class pen-and-paper problem set on probability rules and conditional probability, using the class's own collected datasets as the scenarios.
Explain the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science including history, evolution, AI vs ML vs DL, agent types, and real-world applications
Correlation vs causation – positive and negative correlation, spurious relationships, causal assumptions, analytical pitfalls
Have students manufacture a spurious correlation from their own life data, then argue against their own finding.

Using two datasets about your own life (coffee cups vs marks, sleep hours vs steps, rainfall vs mood), compute a correlation and then write a one-page argument for why causation cannot be claimed from it.
Analyse exploratory data analysis techniques including descriptive statistics, data visualization, outlier detection, trends, and insight generation for decision-making
Interpretation of metrics – context-based evaluation, imbalance handling, business impact of metrics
Give students a printed confusion matrix from a highly imbalanced medical scenario and make them explain it to a non-technical listener.
Given a printed confusion matrix from an imbalanced screening scenario, explain to a non-technical family member why 95% accuracy is misleading. Record their questions and your answers.
Explain the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science including history, evolution, AI vs ML vs DL, agent types, and real-world applications
Supervised vs unsupervised – labeled vs unlabeled data, prediction vs pattern discovery, use cases
Hand each group a bag of mixed physical objects; run one labelled sorting task and one unlabelled clustering task, then discuss what changed.

Take a bag of mixed objects (coins, buttons, leaves, stationery). First sort them using labels the instructor provides, then cluster them with no labels at all. Photograph both results and explain why the groupings differ.
Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow by Aurelien Geron
Regression, classification – continuous output prediction, categorical outcome prediction, real-world applications
Frame problems from hostel and family life and let students argue whether each is regression or classification, including deliberately ambiguous ones.
Frame six real problems from your hostel, home or workplace. Label each as regression or classification, justify it, and identify one problem that could legitimately be framed either way.
Apply data science workflow concepts including CRISP-DM, structured vs unstructured data, data sources, data cleaning, and handling missing values using real-world datasets
Train-test split – model validation, generalization testing, data leakage prevention
Split a physical deck of index cards into train and test piles, then have students predict the held-out week before revealing it.
Write your own 30-day dataset onto index cards. Physically hold out the last seven cards, make written predictions for them, then reveal and compare. Record where and how leakage could have occurred.
Analyse exploratory data analysis techniques including descriptive statistics, data visualization, outlier detection, trends, and insight generation for decision-making
Accuracy, precision, recall – confusion matrix, trade-off analysis, domain-specific metric selection
Have students act as a spam filter on their own messages, then build the confusion matrix by hand from their decisions.

Classify 40 of your own SMS or email messages as spam or not spam by hand, then check against the provider's actual labels. Build the confusion matrix on paper and compute accuracy, precision and recall.
Overfitting vs underfitting – model complexity issues, bias-variance tradeoff, regularization concepts
Draw three fits of increasing complexity through the same scatter of student-collected points and discuss which would survive new data.
Plot your own collected data as a scatter on graph paper. Hand-draw three fitted curves of increasing complexity. Record a 3-minute video explaining to a peer which will generalise and why.
Apply machine learning fundamentals including supervised vs unsupervised learning, regression, classification, train-test split, and evaluation metrics using Python and Jupyter
Bias, fairness – data bias sources, algorithmic bias, ethical implications, fairness metrics
Examine a real selection criterion used inside the institution and ask who it systematically disadvantages.

Examine a real admission, scholarship or placement eligibility criterion at your institution. Identify which group it systematically disadvantages and write a one-page fairness memo proposing a fairer alternative.
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning by Christopher M. Bishop
Transparency, accountability – explainable AI, model interpretability, responsibility in decision making
Pair students to audit each other's models, requiring each to explain a specific prediction to a sceptical peer.

Take one prediction from a classmate's notebook and demand an explanation for it. Write an explainability audit of their work, and receive one for yours. Note every question neither of you could answer.
GDPR basics – data privacy principles, user consent, right to explanation, compliance requirements
Open an actual app privacy policy in class and annotate it against GDPR principles line by line.

Read the full privacy policy of one app installed on your phone. Hand-annotate a printed copy marking where it satisfies and where it strains consent, purpose limitation, data minimisation and the right to explanation. Deliver a 2-minute verdict.
Model misuse – ethical risks, unintended consequences, surveillance concerns, misuse prevention
Ask students to write a short misuse narrative set in their own city, then trace the harm back to a specific design decision.

Write a short story about an AI system deployed in your own city being misused. Identify the single design decision that made the misuse possible and propose the safeguard that would have prevented it.
AI governance – policy frameworks, ethical guidelines, regulatory compliance, organizational oversight
Have students draft an AI usage policy for their own department and take it to a faculty member for real feedback.
Draft a one-page AI usage policy for your own department covering permitted use, disclosure and prohibited use. Obtain written feedback and a signature from one faculty member, then revise it.

Python, Jupyter – programming fundamentals, interactive notebooks, reproducible analysis

Have students digitise the physical data they collected earlier in the course and join it with a second self-collected file.

Ask students to deliberately break their own working notebook in five ways and maintain an error logbook.

sheets.name: Course Description
rows: This course introduces students to the principles, methodologies, and industry practices of Software Testing and Quality Assurance. It covers software testing life cycle (STLC), testing techniques, test automation, defect management, performance testing, security testing, and quality assurance processes. Students gain practical experience with industry-standard testing tools, automation frameworks, and CI/CD integration to ensure software quality in modern development environments.

To equip students with the knowledge and practical skills required to plan, design, execute, automate and manage software testing activities while applying quality assurance practices to develop reliable, secure, and high-quality software systems.

Understand software testing fundamentals including testing principles, SDLC, STLC, defect lifecycle, defect clustering, pesticide paradox, test planning, test closure, test documentation (Test Plan, Test Case, RTM), testing levels (Unit, Integration, System, UAT), and software review techniques.

Apply manual testing techniques by designing and executing test cases using Equivalence Partitioning, Boundary Value Analysis (BVA), Statement, Branch and Path Coverage, Smoke, Sanity, Performance and Security Testing, while performing execution-based testing and peer test reviews.

Analyze software quality by performing Selenium WebDriver automation, automation frameworks, REST API testing, JMeter performance testing, Jira and TestRail defect management, Jenkins CI/CD pipelines, regression automation, bug lifecycle management, test estimation, defect density and test coverage analysis.

Prepare a comprehensive Software Test Plan and Requirement Traceability Matrix (RTM) for an Online Shopping System.

Students will analyze the Software Requirement Specification (SRS), identify functional and non-functional requirements, prepare a professional Test Plan including scope, objectives, testing strategy, test environment, resources, risks, entry/exit criteria, schedule, and develop an RTM mapping requirements to test cases.
Rubric: Test Plan completeness (40%), RTM accuracy (30%), Documentation quality & presentation (30%)
Design comprehensive manual test cases using Equivalence Partitioning (EP) and Boundary Value Analysis (BVA) for a Banking/Login application.
Students will identify valid and invalid input conditions, prepare positive and negative test cases, define expected results, assign priorities, and justify the selected test design techniques.
Rubric: Test case coverage (40%), Correct application of EP/BVA (40%), Documentation quality (20%)
Perform manual testing on a web application and generate a professional defect report.

Students will execute prepared test cases on an assigned application, identify defects, classify severity and priority, reproduce defects, capture evidence, and prepare bug reports using standard defect templates.
Rubric: Test execution (40%), Defect identification & reporting (40%), Documentation (20%)
Develop an automation testing framework using Selenium WebDriver and TestNG.

Students will automate login, registration, search, and logout functionalities using Selenium WebDriver, implement Page Object Model (POM), reusable utilities, assertions, and generate HTML execution reports.
Rubric: Framework design (40%), Automation implementation (40%), Code quality & reporting (20%)
Perform REST API Testing using Postman for a public REST API.
Students will create API collections, validate HTTP methods, authentication, status codes, response payloads, headers, and automate test execution using Collection Runner with assertions.
Rubric: API coverage (40%), Assertions & validation (30%), Documentation (30%)
Analyze the performance of a web application using Apache JMeter.
Students will create load test scenarios, simulate concurrent users, measure response time, throughput, latency, and identify potential performance bottlenecks through result analysis.
Rubric: Test configuration (40%), Result analysis (40%), Performance report (20%)
Conduct Risk-Based Testing and perform a basic OWASP security assessment for an e-commerce application.

Students will identify business risks, prioritize testing based on risk exposure, analyze common web vulnerabilities (SQL Injection, XSS, Broken Authentication), recommend mitigation strategies, and prepare a security assessment report.
Rubric: Risk analysis (40%), Security recommendations (30%), Technical justification (30%)
Design and implement a complete End-to-End Software Testing Solution integrating Manual Testing, Automation, API Testing, Performance Testing, CI/CD, and Defect Management.

Students will execute a real-world testing project by preparing test artefacts, automating functional tests, testing APIs, performing load testing, managing defects using Jira, integrating automated execution with Jenkins, creating testing dashboards, and presenting project outcomes.
Rubric: End-to-end implementation (40%), Tool integration & automation (30%), Documentation, presentation & viva (30%)
